subQuestions.questionText:
Match the concept in COLUMN A with the most appropriate term in COLUMN B by writing only the matching letter (A–E) next to the question number.

COLUMN A: An expense incurred for the year that has not yet been paid.

COLUMN B options:
A. Prepaid expense
B. Accrued expense
C. Income received in advance
D. Depreciation
E. Provision for bad debts
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B — Accrued expense (1 mark)
An accrued expense is an expense that has been incurred during the financial period but has not yet been paid by year-end. It is recognised as a current liability in the Statement of Financial Position.

subQuestions.questionText:
Match the concept in COLUMN A with the most appropriate term in COLUMN B by writing only the matching letter (A–E) next to the question number.

COLUMN A: Income received for a service that will only be rendered in the next financial year.

COLUMN B options:
A. Prepaid expense
B. Accrued expense
C. Income received in advance
D. Depreciation
E. Provision for bad debts
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C — Income received in advance (1 mark)
When income is received in the current period for a service or benefit that will only be provided in the next financial period, it must be deferred. It is recognised as a current liability (income received in advance) and only recognised as income when earned.

subQuestions.questionText:
Match the concept in COLUMN A with the most appropriate term in COLUMN B by writing only the matching letter (A–E) next to the question number.

COLUMN A: An asset that loses value over time due to wear and tear.

COLUMN B options:
A. Prepaid expense
B. Accrued expense
C. Income received in advance
D. Depreciation
E. Provision for bad debts
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D — Depreciation (1 mark)
Depreciation is the systematic allocation of the cost of a tangible fixed asset over its useful life to reflect the loss in value due to wear and tear, usage and obsolescence.

Mark 1: R 38 000 (opening) + R 9 000 (current year, from 2.1.3) = R 47 000 ✓

Mark 2: Cost R 80 000 − Accumulated depreciation R 47 000 = R 33 000 ✓

Step 3 — Compare selling price to carrying value:
Mark 3: Selling price R 28 000 ✓

subQuestions.questionText:
Calculate the Acid-test ratio at 28 February 2026.

Current liabilities: Creditors R 298 000 + Shareholders for dividends R 315 000 = R 613 000

subQuestions.questionText:
LIQUIDITY: Comment on the liquidity position of Sibonelo Limited. Quote THREE indicators (with figures and trends). Indicate whether shareholders should be concerned.

Key figures (Information 6): Current ratio: 1,8:1 (2026) vs 2,4:1 (2025), industry 1,7:1. Acid-test: 0,7:1 (2026) vs 1,3:1 (2025), industry 0,9:1. Stock turnover: 8,4 times (2026) vs 6,1 times (2025). Debtors collection: 32 days (2026) vs 44 days (2025). Creditors payment: 60 days (2026) vs 45 days (2025), industry 55 days.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark allocation: figure quoted ✓ + trend identified ✓ + judgement ✓ per indicator. THREE indicators required (8 marks total).

Concern: Liquidity has DETERIORATED significantly.

Indicator 1 — Current ratio:
• Figure: dropped from 2,4 : 1 to 1,8 : 1 ✓✓
• Trend: still above industry (1,7 : 1) but trending negatively
• Judgement: declining liquidity buffer

Indicator 2 — Acid-test ratio (the strongest red flag):
• Figure: fell from 1,3 : 1 to 0,7 : 1 ✓✓
• Trend: well below industry average of 0,9 : 1, and below the safe rule of 1 : 1
• Judgement: company relies on selling inventory to meet short-term obligations — this is risky

Indicator 3 — Stock turnover (or Creditors payment period):
• Stock turnover increased from 6,1 to 8,4 times ✓ — stock moves faster, but combined with low liquidity may indicate inventory running low
• OR Creditors payment period rose from 45 to 60 days ✓ — Sibonelo is paying suppliers more slowly, propping up liquidity but damaging supplier relationships

Judgement (overall): YES — shareholders SHOULD be concerned. The acid-test deterioration is the strongest red flag. ✓

questions.title: Audit, Corporate Governance, Ethics & Internal Control

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to INFORMATION 8 (Auditor's report). What type of audit report has been issued? Quote ONE phrase from the report to support your answer.

INFORMATION 8 — Extract from Independent Auditor's Report (Sibonelo Limited):
'Basis for Qualified Opinion: During our audit we were unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the existence and valuation of inventory amounting to R 1 240 000... Qualified Opinion: In our opinion, EXCEPT for the possible effects of the matter described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion paragraph, the financial statements present fairly...'
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Type of audit report: QUALIFIED audit opinion ✓

Mark 2: Quote (any ONE) ✓
• 'Basis for Qualified Opinion' OR
• 'In our opinion, except for the possible effects' OR
• 'we were unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence'

[Award 1 mark for correctly identifying 'Qualified' and 1 mark for any valid supporting quote from the report. Reject vague descriptions — the actual phrase from the report must be quoted.]

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the implication of this type of report for the shareholders.
subQuestions.memoText:
Implication for shareholders ✓✓ (any TWO valid points, 1 mark each):

• The auditors could NOT verify R 1 240 000 of inventory.
• Shareholders cannot fully rely on the inventory figure or any related figures (e.g. cost of sales, gross profit, stock turnover rate).
• Decision-making by shareholders (e.g. whether to vote for dividends, buy/sell shares) is impaired due to the unreliability of those specific figures.
• Shareholder confidence in management's stewardship may decline.
• The qualified opinion may negatively affect the share price.

[Award 2 marks for any TWO well-explained implications. The point must specifically relate to shareholders, not to the company or auditors generally.]

subQuestions.questionText: State ONE specific corrective action the directors should take so that an unqualified report can be issued next year.
subQuestions.memoText:
ONE specific corrective action ✓✓ (any ONE well-explained, 2 marks):

Improve internal controls over inventory:
• Implement perpetual inventory records (continuous tracking system).
• Conduct regular physical stock counts reconciled to the ledger / GRN records.
• Enforce segregation of duties for stock receipts and stock issues.
• Appoint an internal auditor to oversee the stock cycle and verify counts.
• Install CCTV / access control in the warehouse to prevent shrinkage.
• Use barcoded inventory items with electronic scanning.

[Award 2 marks for ONE specific, well-explained action. Vague answers like 'check inventory better' earn only 1 mark. The action must specifically address why the auditor could not verify the inventory.]

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to INFORMATION 9 (Internal Control & Ethics). Explain why scenario (a) — Mr Khumalo selling his shares — is a serious ethical and legal concern. Use the correct accounting/legal term.

Scenario (a): Mr S. Khumalo, the Financial Director, sold 25 000 of his personal shares in the company on 14 January 2026 — two weeks BEFORE Sibonelo Limited issued a SENS announcement that profits would fall by 18% for the half-year.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mr Khumalo's behaviour is INSIDER TRADING ✓ (1 mark for correct legal term)

Explanation (1 mark):
• Insider trading is illegal in terms of the Financial Markets Act (s 78).
• He used non-public material information (the impending profit warning) to avoid losses on his own shares — this is unfair to other investors who didn't have the same information.
• It is also a breach of his fiduciary duty as a director (Companies Act s 76; King IV) ✓

[Mark 1: Identifying the term 'insider trading'. Mark 2: A coherent explanation of WHY it's wrong (use of non-public information / breach of fiduciary duty / unfair advantage). Both marks required for full credit.]

subQuestions.questionText:
State TWO specific internal control measures that should be implemented to prevent the situation in scenario (b) from recurring.

Scenario (b): The Internal Auditor reported that 12 invoices totalling R 246 000 had been paid to a supplier, 'Quick-Fix Trading', with no supporting delivery notes. Quick-Fix Trading is a close corporation owned by Mr Khumalo's spouse.
subQuestions.memoText:
TWO specific internal control measures ✓✓✓✓ (2 marks per measure, max 4):

Measure 1 — Three-way matching:
• No payment may be processed without three-way matching: Purchase Order + Delivery Note + Supplier Invoice ✓✓
• This would have prevented payment because there were no delivery notes.

Measure 2 — Segregation of duties:
• The person approving suppliers must not be the same person processing payments ✓✓
• Two different signatories for cheque/EFT authorisation.

Measure 3 — Conflict-of-interest register:
• Directors must declare related-party suppliers (Mr Khumalo's spouse owning Quick-Fix Trading) ✓✓
• Disclosure required by the Companies Act and King IV.

Measure 4 — Dual authorisation:
• Mandatory authorisation by TWO senior officials for any payment above a set threshold (e.g. R 50 000) ✓✓

[Award 2 marks per WELL-EXPLAINED measure (max 4 marks total). 1 mark only for a measure stated without explanation. Accept any TWO of the above or other reasonable answers.]
subQuestions.topic: Internal Control - Payments and Conflict of Interest

subQuestions.questionText:
Comment on whether the CEO's response in scenario (c) complies with the Companies Act and King IV principles.

Scenario (c): The CEO, Ms J. Maboea, has refused to disclose her director's remuneration in the Notes to the Financial Statements. She insists this is 'private information not relevant to ordinary shareholders'.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: NO — the CEO is wrong ✓

Mark 2: Companies Act / IFRS basis:
• The Companies Act (s 30) AND IFRS require that directors' remuneration be disclosed in the annual financial statements ✓
• Disclosure of each director's salary, bonuses, fees and benefits is mandatory.

Mark 3: King IV basis:
• King IV Principle 14 (Fair, responsible and transparent remuneration) requires full disclosure to shareholders ✓
• Shareholders hold directors accountable — they need to see what executives are paid relative to performance.
• Refusal to disclose breaches both legal and governance requirements and could trigger a qualified audit report.

Answer: NO. The CEO's refusal violates the Companies Act, IFRS and King IV. Full disclosure is mandatory.

[Award 1 mark for the correct judgement (NO/wrong), and 2 marks for citing TWO valid legal/governance reasons. Total = 3 marks.]
